section.title: The Lord's Prayer and the Woes
section.sectionRationale: Asked to teach His disciples to pray, Jesus gives them the Father's prayer and urges bold, persistent asking, promising that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. He then answers the charge that He casts out demons by Beelzebul, warns against a merely swept and empty life, and, at a Pharisee's table, pronounces woes on hypocrisy that keeps the outside clean while the inside is full of greed. Prayer to the Father and integrity of heart belong together.
section.thesis: The kingdom comes as children learn to pray to a Father who delights to give, and it is opposed by a religion of clean outsides and cold hearts, so Jesus calls His people to persistent prayer, to the finger of God at work, and to a righteousness that begins within.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the pattern of prayer; the call to ask, seek, and knock; the finger of God and the divided kingdom; the sign of Jonah and the lamp of the body; and the woes on the Pharisees and experts in the law.

verses.text: One day in a place where Jesus had just finished praying, one of His disciples requested, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.”
So Jesus told them, “When you pray, say: ‘{{pater|Father}}, {{hagiazo|hallowed}} be Your name. Your {{basileia|kingdom}} come.
Give us each day our daily bread.
And forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who sins against us. And lead us not into temptation.’”

units.label: Ask, seek, knock
units.note: how much more will your Father give the Spirit

verses.text: Then Jesus said to them, “Suppose one of you goes to his friend at midnight and says, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread,
because a friend of mine has come to me on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.’
And suppose the one inside answers, ‘Do not bother me. My door is already shut, and my children and I are in bed. I cannot get up to give you anything.’
I tell you, even though he will not get up to provide for him because of his friendship, yet because of the man’s persistence, he will get up and give him as much as he needs.
So I tell you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks, the door will be opened.
What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead?
Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion?
So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the {{pneuma|Holy Spirit}} to those who ask Him!”

units.label: The finger of God and the divided kingdom
units.note: the kingdom of God has come upon you

verses.text: One day Jesus was driving out a demon that was mute. And when the demon was gone, the man who had been mute spoke. The crowds were amazed,
but some of them said, “It is by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons, that He drives out demons.”
And others tested Him by demanding a sign from heaven.
Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and a house divided against a house will fall.
If Satan is divided against himself, how can his kingdom stand? After all, you say that I drive out demons by Beelzebul.
And if I drive out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons drive them out? So then, they will be your judges.
But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the {{basileia|kingdom}} of God has come upon you.
When a strong man, fully armed, guards his house, his possessions are secure.
But when someone stronger attacks and overpowers him, he takes away the armor in which the man trusted, and then he divides up his plunder.
He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters.
When an unclean spirit comes out of a man, it passes through arid places seeking rest and does not find it. Then it says, ‘I will return to the house I left.’
On its return, it finds the house swept clean and put in order.
Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they go in and dwell there. And the final plight of that man is worse than the first.”

units.label: True blessedness, the sign of Jonah, and the lamp
units.note: hear the word of God and obey it

verses.text: As Jesus was saying these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said, “Blessed is the womb that bore You, and blessed are the breasts that nursed You!”
But He replied, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it.”
As the crowds were increasing, Jesus said, “This is a wicked generation. It demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah.
For as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of Man will be a sign to this generation.

The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here.
The men of Nineveh will stand at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now One greater than Jonah is here.
No one lights a lamp and puts it in a cellar or under a basket. Instead, he sets it on a stand, so those who enter can see the light.
Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eyes are good, your whole body also is full of light. But when they are bad, your body is full of darkness.
Be careful, then, that the light within you is not darkness.
So if your whole body is full of light, with no part of it in darkness, you will be radiant, as though a lamp were shining on you.”

units.label: The woes on the Pharisees and the experts
units.note: you clean the outside, but inside is greed

verses.text: As Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee invited Him to dine with him; so He went in and reclined at the table.
But the Pharisee was surprised to see that Jesus did not first wash before the meal.
Then the Lord said, “Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness.
You fools! Did not the One who made the outside make the inside as well?
But give as alms the things that are within you, and behold, everything will be clean for you.
Woe to you Pharisees! For you pay tithes of mint, rue, and every herb, but you disregard justice and the love of God. You should have practiced the latter without neglecting the former.
Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the chief seats in the synagogues and the greetings in the marketplaces.
Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, which men walk over without even noticing.”
One of the experts in the law told Him, “Teacher, when You say these things, You insult us as well.”
“Woe to you as well, experts in the law!” He replied. “For you weigh men down with heavy burdens, but you yourselves will not lift a finger to lighten their load.
Woe to you! For you build tombs for the prophets, but it was your fathers who killed them.
So you are witnesses consenting to the deeds of your fathers: They killed the prophets, and you build their tombs.
Because of this, the wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles; some of them they will kill and others they will persecute.’
As a result, this generation will be charged with the blood of all the prophets that has been shed since the foundation of the world,
from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, all of it will be charged to this generation.
Woe to you experts in the law! For you have taken away the key to knowledge. You yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who were entering.”
As Jesus went on from there, the scribes and Pharisees began to oppose Him bitterly and to ply Him with questions about many things,
waiting to catch Him in something He might say.

pater.gloss: Father. Jesus teaches His disciples to open prayer with the intimate address Father, the Aramaic Abba behind it, drawing them into His own relationship of trust with God. Prayer here is not the plea of slaves but the confident asking of children.

hagiazo.gloss: To hallow, to treat as holy, to set apart. To pray hallowed be Your name is to ask that God's name and reputation be honored and revered, in us and in all the earth, the first and governing petition of the prayer.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, kingship, reign. The prayer longs for God's kingdom to come, and Jesus declares that where He casts out demons by the finger of God, that kingdom has already broken in. His mighty works are the reign of God arriving in person.

pneuma.gloss: Holy Spirit. Luke's version of the ask, seek, knock promise names the best gift the Father gives to those who ask: the Holy Spirit Himself. Prayer's surest answer is not merely things but God's own presence and power.

basic.context: Seeing Jesus pray, a disciple asks to be taught, and Jesus gives the pattern we call the Lord's Prayer: address God as Father, hallow His name, seek His kingdom, ask for daily bread, forgiveness, and rescue from temptation. He then tells of a friend at midnight to urge bold, persistent asking, and promises that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. When accused of casting out demons by Beelzebul, He shows that a divided Satan would fall and that His exorcisms are the finger of God, the kingdom breaking in. He warns against an empty, swept-clean life, points to the sign of Jonah, and at a Pharisee's table pronounces woes on those who clean the outside while the inside is full of greed.
basic.hermeneutics: Let the prayer set the key: everything flows from calling God Father. The parable of the midnight friend and the ask, seek, knock sayings are about the Father's readiness to give, climaxing in the gift of the Spirit. The Beelzebul controversy and the woes then expose the alternative: religion that resists the kingdom and polishes the surface while the heart is unclean.
basic.originalLanguages: The prayer begins with pater, Father, and asks that His name be hagiazo, hallowed, and His basileia, kingdom, come. That same kingdom, Jesus says, has come upon them where the finger of God drives out demons. And the crown of answered prayer, in Luke's wording, is the pneuma hagion, the Holy Spirit, the Father's best gift.
basic.typology: Jonah three days in the fish and then preaching to Nineveh foreshadows the Son of Man's death, resurrection, and the call to repentance. Solomon's wisdom that drew the Queen of the South points to One greater than Solomon now present.
basic.christ: Jesus is the one who prays and teaches prayer, the Son who makes God our Father. He is the stronger man who binds the strong and plunders his house, the finger of God bringing in the kingdom, the sign of Jonah in His death and rising, and the One greater than Solomon and Jonah standing before them.
basic.god: God is the Father who welcomes His children's bold asking and gives good gifts, supremely the Holy Spirit. He is holy, His name to be hallowed, His kingdom to come. And He is the searching God who cares about the inside of the cup, not merely the outside.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 6 gives the fuller form of the prayer. Romans 8 shows the Spirit crying Abba, Father, in us. Exodus 8 names the finger of God. 1 Samuel 16 reminds us that the Lord looks on the heart.
basic.oneStory: The kingdom comes as children learn to pray to a giving Father and as the stronger Son plunders the house of the enemy. It is resisted by hearts that clean the outside and neglect the love of God, so Jesus calls us to persistent prayer and to a righteousness that starts within.

context.literary:
Luke 11 is built as a sequence of three conversations with three audiences, and the changes of audience carry the argument. The first part, verses 1 to 13, is private teaching to disciples about prayer. The second, verses 14 to 36, is a public controversy in front of crowds, in which Jesus answers the charge of working with Satan and then turns to the demand for a sign. The third, verses 37 to 54, takes place in a Pharisee's home, with Jesus reclining at the table, and ends with open hostility. Each panel moves from invitation to refusal, and the whole chapter asks which side of the kingdom a hearer is standing on.

Several small links hold it together. The man at midnight asks for bread for a guest in verses 5 to 8, and Jesus later sits at a table where the host's concern is only the surface of the dishes. The theme of the 'house' recurs, in the house shut at midnight, the strong man's house plundered in verse 22, the swept and empty house in verses 24 to 26, and the Pharisee's house where the inside is not clean. The theme of the 'eye' and the 'light' in verses 33 to 36 is the hinge between the controversy and the meal: the problem is not a lack of evidence but a darkened eye. Even the interruption in verses 27 and 28, where a woman blesses Jesus' mother, serves the pattern, because Jesus redirects blessing to those who hear the word and obey it.

Within Luke's travel narrative this chapter is the first time the opposition hardens into a plot. Verses 53 and 54 say the scribes and Pharisees 'began to oppose Him bitterly' and wait to catch Him out. The prayer at the beginning therefore stands as the counterweight to everything that follows: a few lines to teach us how to approach God, set before a long catalogue of the ways people refuse Him.
context.historical:
Verse 1 shows Jesus at prayer before a disciple asks to be taught. Luke records Jesus praying at the major points of His ministry, at His baptism in Luke 3:21, on the mountain before choosing the Twelve in Luke 6:12, and frequently in solitude, Luke 5:16. The disciple's remark that John taught his disciples to pray shows that a rabbi's followers were identified by the prayer that he gave them. What Jesus supplies is short and plain, five petitions in Luke, and is addressed with the single word 'Father.' It is striking that Jesus uses Father for God so directly in a world where the divine name was treated with great reverence; Paul says in Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6 that believers cry 'Abba, Father' by the Spirit.

The midnight scene reflects the hospitality code of a village. A traveller arrives late, and the host has no bread left to set out. Everyone in the village would have shared that shame, and refusal to help would have disgraced the whole neighborhood. The sleeping household, with children in bed, pictures a one-room home in which opening the door means rousing everyone.

The charge about Beelzebul reflects a world in which exorcism was known and had to be explained. The name is probably related to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron consulted in 2 Kings 1:2, and it had become a title for the prince of demons. Jesus' reply uses a clever fact: Jewish exorcists were practising among His critics, verse 19, so the accusation, if consistent, would also condemn them. The sign of Jonah and the Queen of the South draw on two foreigners whom Israel's own records celebrated, the Ninevites who repented in Jonah 3:5 and the queen who came to hear Solomon in 1 Kings 10:1.

The meal scene turns on purity customs. Hand washing and the careful cleansing of vessels were marks of devout observance, and tithing even small garden herbs, mint and rue, verse 42, followed the law's tithe of the produce of the land in Leviticus 27:30. The 'unmarked graves' of verse 44 refer to the law that a person who touches a grave is unclean for seven days, Numbers 19:16. A grave no one can see defiles the unwary, and in the same way the leaders pass on contamination without knowing it.
context.canonical:
The Lord's Prayer sits at a junction of Old and New Testaments. Calling God Father was not new in Israel, but it had been rare and corporate, as in Isaiah 63:16 and Hosea 11:1. Jesus teaches His disciples to use it personally, and Paul says that is what the Spirit of sonship does, Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6. The petition for 'daily bread' recalls the manna that fell each day in the wilderness, Exodus 16:4, and the prayer for forgiveness ties itself to the way we treat others, which Luke 6:37 and Matthew 18:21-35 develop.

The 'finger of God' of verse 20 reaches back to Exodus 8:19, where Pharaoh's own magicians admit that the plagues are God's doing, and to Exodus 31:18, where the finger of God wrote the tablets of the law. Matthew's parallel says 'Spirit of God,' Matthew 12:28, and it helps to read the two together: the same power that wrote the law and broke Pharaoh now breaks Satan's hold. The strong man imagery recalls Isaiah 49:24-25, where the LORD promises that the captives of the mighty will be taken and the plunder of the tyrant retrieved.

The Jonah, Nineveh and Queen of the South sayings are rooted in Jonah 3:5 and 1 Kings 10:1, and Matthew 12:40 adds the three days in the fish as a pointer to the burial and resurrection. The final woe is the climax of a long canonical pattern. 'From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah' spans from Genesis 4:8 to 2 Chronicles 24:20-22, and since Chronicles stands last in the Hebrew order of the Scriptures, the phrase covers the entire Old Testament from first book to last. Nehemiah 9:26 names the same history of killing prophets, and Luke 13:34 will repeat the charge over Jerusalem.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants the reader to see the entire chapter as one question: what is the right way to come near to God, and what is the wrong way? In the first section a disciple learns it. The pattern prayer is short, addressed to a Father, and given in a style that cannot be used to impress anyone. The parable of the friend and the sayings about asking move in the same direction, away from fear and toward confident, repeated petition. The comparison between earthly fathers who give good things and the heavenly Father who gives the Holy Spirit is meant to dissolve the suspicion that God is reluctant.

In the second and third sections Luke shows the alternative. Some of the crowd explain Jesus away as a servant of Satan, and others demand a sign, though a man has just been freed from a demon before their eyes. The Pharisee and the legal experts keep the rules and polish the surface and miss justice and the love of God. The author's aim is to leave the reader unable to remain neutral. Verse 23 puts it as bluntly as it can be put: whoever is not with Him is against Him. The chapter calls readers to move from watching Jesus to hearing Him and acting on His word, which is how verse 28 describes true blessedness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The Lord's Prayer is given as a pattern, 'When you pray, say,' and the church has rightly used it both as words to pray and as a template for what to ask. Luke's shorter form shows that it was never meant as a mechanical formula, since Matthew's form is longer. The midnight friend and the ask, seek, knock sayings use present-tense commands, which suggest continuing action, 'keep asking,' and Jesus gives them as standing instructions for His followers, not as a one-time promise.

The Beelzebul controversy and the dinner at the Pharisee's table describe particular events, but what is said in them is prescriptive wherever the same attitudes are found. Anyone who explains good works as evil, or who demands more signs while refusing the one given, stands where those crowds stood. The woes were spoken to particular groups of Pharisees and legal experts, and it would be a mistake to turn them into a general verdict on any people or movement. They describe a posture of the heart that can belong to anyone who has a religious reputation to protect, including a reader of Luke.

debates.question: What does the promise that everyone who asks receives mean?

views.label: The Father gives good gifts, supremely the Spirit
views.case: Luke frames the promise around a Father who will not give a snake for a fish, and names the Holy Spirit as the gift; the assurance is that God answers with what is truly good, not every request as asked.

views.label: A blanket guarantee of whatever we request
views.case: Some read ask and receive as an unconditional promise of any desire, but Luke's own wording, culminating in the Spirit, and the wider teaching of Scripture qualify it by the Father's wisdom and goodness.

debates.bearing: Persistent prayer is warmly encouraged, yet its surest and highest answer is God Himself by His Spirit, so we ask boldly while trusting the Father to give what is good.

debates.question: What is the sign of Jonah in Luke?

views.label: Jonah's preaching and Nineveh's repentance
views.case: Luke stresses that Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites who repented, so the sign is the Son of Man's call to repentance that this generation refuses.

views.label: The death and resurrection
views.case: Read alongside Matthew's fuller saying about three days in the fish, the sign includes the Son of Man's burial and rising, the ultimate vindication offered to an unbelieving generation.

debates.bearing: Both point to a generation without excuse: it has One greater than Jonah preaching repentance and, in due course, rising from the dead, yet still it demands a sign.

debates.question: Does 'lead us not into temptation' mean God might tempt us?

views.label: It asks God to keep us from trials we would fail
views.case: The Greek word peirasmos covers both testing and temptation. Jesus tells His disciples in Luke 22:40 to 'pray that you will not enter into temptation,' and James 1:13 says God tempts no one. On this reading the petition is a plea not to be brought to a test too hard for us, a prayer of humble self-distrust.

views.label: It asks God not to let the trial become a fall
views.case: Because God does lead His people into hard places, as the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness in Luke 4:1-2, the petition asks that the testing not end in sin. Matthew's longer form, 'but deliver us from the evil one,' Matthew 6:13, which the BSB footnote notes also appears in later manuscripts of Luke, makes the same turn from the trial to rescue.

debates.bearing: Both views honour James 1:13: God is never the author of evil. The petition is the plea of children who know how weak they are, and it belongs naturally beside the daily bread and the forgiveness, which are also requests for help we cannot supply ourselves.

study.originalLanguages:
The prayer in Luke is built from five brief imperatives. 'Hallowed be Your name' uses hagiasthetō, a passive verb that asks God Himself to make His name holy, to show it as holy in the world. The next request, 'Your kingdom come,' is a petition for the thing Jesus is already announcing. In Luke 'give us each day our daily bread' is expressed with a present imperative, didou, which fits a daily and repeated asking, while the word translated 'daily,' epiousios, is found in the New Testament only in the two versions of this prayer. Its precise meaning is not settled, and 'for the coming day,' 'for today' and 'needed for existence' are all proposed, which is why the BSB says 'daily.' The forgiveness petition in Luke 11:4 speaks first of 'sins,' hamartias, and then says we forgive everyone who is literally 'indebted to us,' opheilonti, so Luke joins the picture of sin as wrong and sin as debt.

The verbs in the ask, seek and knock saying in verses 9 and 10 are present imperatives: aiteite, zeteite, krouete. The sense is to keep asking, keep seeking and keep knocking. The same sentiment sits behind the parable of the friend, where the BSB renders the neighbour's 'persistence' in verse 8. The Greek word, anaideia, literally means shamelessness, and readers have long argued whether it describes the asker's bold refusal to be embarrassed or the host's reluctance to be shamed before the village. Either way, the argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if a grudging friend will rise, the generous Father will certainly give.

In verse 20 the kingdom 'has come upon you,' using ephthasen, an aorist verb which implies that the kingdom has arrived and overtaken them. In Luke 10:9 and 11 the verb engiken, 'is near,' described the kingdom as close at hand, so the movement from 'near' to 'come upon' is deliberate. Verse 34 says that the eye is the lamp of the body. The words for 'good' and 'bad' eyes are haplous, which suggests single or sound, and ponēros, which means evil or diseased, and in Jewish idiom an 'evil eye' described a grudging, stingy or envious look, as the BSB's 'stingy' in Proverbs 23:6 reflects. Finally, verse 41 is notoriously difficult: 'give as alms the things that are within you.' The Greek phrase ta enonta means 'what is within,' and some scholars suggest the underlying Aramaic could be read as either 'cleanse' or 'give alms,' which would explain the parallel in Matthew 23:26 that speaks of cleansing the inside. The sense in either case is that true purity begins with a generous heart.

typology.type: Jonah the sign to Nineveh, Luke 11:29-32
typology.fulfillment: Jonah was a prophet sent to a pagan city whose people believed God and repented in sackcloth, Jonah 3:5. Jesus says the Son of Man will be a sign to this generation as Jonah was to the Ninevites. Matthew's fuller form links the sign to the fish and to the three days of burial, Matthew 12:40, and the pattern of a rescue from the deep points to the resurrection. In Christ the correspondence is intensified, because 'One greater than Jonah is here.' The type falls short in that Jonah was a reluctant messenger who resented the mercy shown, Jonah 4:1, while Jesus is the willing Son who gives His life for the city that rejects Him.

typology.type: Solomon's wisdom and the Queen of the South, 1 Kings 10:1-9
typology.fulfillment: The queen travelled from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, the greatest king of Israel, and she went home praising God. Jesus says that 'One greater than Solomon is here.' Christ is the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24 and 30, and in Colossians 2:3 all the treasures of wisdom are hidden in Him. The type falls short because Solomon's wisdom was partial and his later years turned from the LORD, 1 Kings 11:4, while Christ is faultless wisdom in person and the kingdom He brings has no end.

typology.type: The finger of God in Egypt and at Sinai
typology.fulfillment: The magicians of Egypt confessed at the third plague that it was 'the finger of God,' Exodus 8:19, and the tablets of the law were 'inscribed by the finger of God,' Exodus 31:18. Jesus applies the phrase to the exorcism of the mute man: the power that humbled Pharaoh and gave the law is now at work to free a man held by a demon. The exodus pattern of liberation reaches its peak in Christ's victory over the real tyrant, Hebrews 2:14-15. The type falls short because the plagues freed Israel from a political oppressor, whereas Jesus frees people from the one who holds the power of death.

typology.type: The strong man bound and plundered, Luke 11:21-22
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 49:24-25 asks whether plunder can be taken from the mighty and then answers that the LORD will retrieve the captives of the tyrant. Jesus uses the parable of the strong man to describe His own victory: the 'stronger' one has overcome the fully armed guardian and is dividing the spoil. Isaiah 53:12 pictures the Servant dividing the spoils with the strong because He poured out His life unto death. The escalation comes at the cross, Colossians 2:15, where the rulers and authorities are disarmed. The picture falls short if it suggests Satan was defeated merely by force, because the Servant wins by giving up His life, as Isaiah 53:12 itself says.

study.christ:
This chapter reveals Christ in several roles that the basic summary only touches, and each is anchored in a verse. In verse 1 He is praying, and the Gospel of Luke has shown Him doing this at every important point. The Son who teaches the disciples to say 'Father' is the one who prays that way Himself, Luke 10:21 and 22:42. When He invites His followers to call God Father, He is bringing them into His own relationship, which Galatians 4:6 says is shared by the Spirit of His Son in our hearts.

In verses 14 to 23 He is the stronger one. The accusation that He works for Satan is answered by the logic that a divided kingdom cannot stand, and then by a claim: the kingdom of God has come upon them in the exorcism. The significance is more than a single healing. The strong man's house is plundered because the stronger one has already entered it. Jesus sees His whole ministry as that invasion, and this is why 'he who is not with Me is against Me.' A neutral position is not available when the kingdom is arriving.

In verses 29 to 32 He is the sign. He calls Himself the Son of Man who will be a sign to the generation, and He places Himself above Jonah and above Solomon. Jonah's name, Solomon's wisdom, the kings and prophets who came and went, all point to someone greater. Matthew spells out that the sign includes three days in the heart of the earth, Matthew 12:40. Luke's version is shorter, and the sign of Jonah may be the call to repentance, as Luke's wording stresses. Either way, the sign is the Son of Man Himself.

In verses 39 to 52 He speaks as the one who sees the heart. His diagnosis of the Pharisees' outward cleanliness reaches back to the word of the LORD to Samuel that He 'sees the heart,' 1 Samuel 16:7. The final woe adds that the wisdom of God has sent prophets and apostles, and the language of verse 49 places Jesus within the long line of those sent and rejected, though greater than all of them. The cost of this will be seen in Luke 13:33-34, where the city that kills the prophets will kill Him too. The one who has taught us to pray to the Father, who plunders the strong man and who exposes the unclean heart is also the one who will be rejected on the road to Jerusalem.
study.god:
The chapter's God is first of all a Father, and the whole prayer is shaped by what that means. He is holy, so that His name must be hallowed and no one may treat Him lightly. He is a king, and His kingdom is the thing we are told to ask for, so the prayer places God's rule before our needs. He is a provider, who gives bread for each day. He forgives, and He expects those who are forgiven to forgive. He is a guardian who leads His people away from the trials that would overcome them. Across its petitions the prayer sets out the doctrine of God as holy, sovereign, generous and merciful.

Verse 13 then compares God to human fathers, 'if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children.' The comparison is not an equation, since the argument runs from the lesser to the greater, and Jesus does not say that the fathers' imperfect care exhausts God's. It says that He is better than the best of them. Luke names the gift as the Holy Spirit, in contrast with Matthew 7:11, 'good things,' and the difference is instructive: God's best gift is Himself. That is a distinctively Trinitarian statement, with the Father giving, the Son teaching, and the Spirit being given.

The chapter also shows God as the searcher of hearts. He is not fooled by outward cleanliness, and the lament that people pay tithes of mint and rue while neglecting 'justice and the love of God,' verse 42, sets before us a God who weighs inner things above ritual, as Micah 6:8 and Hosea 6:6 had already said. The same God is the Creator of both inside and outside, 'Did not the One who made the outside make the inside as well?' verse 40. He is therefore concerned with the whole person.

Finally, the chapter shows God as just. The blood of the prophets since the foundation of the world will be charged to a generation that treats them the way earlier ones did, verses 50 and 51. The judgment is neither random nor sudden, since patient messengers precede it. For worship, the chapter teaches us to begin with 'Father,' to keep asking, and to let God look inside the cup.

crossReferences.note: Matthew's longer form of the prayer adds 'Our Father in heaven,' 'Your will be done,' and 'deliver us from the evil one.' Reading both shows that Jesus taught a pattern and not a fixed script, and each Gospel preserves a faithful form of it. Matthew gives the fuller liturgical version, and Luke gives a compact one.

The persistent widow and the unjust judge teach that disciples 'need to pray at all times and not lose heart.' Like the midnight friend, the story argues from the unwilling human to the willing God, and Luke's two parables are best read together as a pair about persistence.

Paul says believers did not receive a spirit of slavery but the Spirit of sonship, by whom they cry 'Abba! Father!' That is the lasting fruit of verse 13: the Father gives the Holy Spirit, and the Spirit enables the very prayer Jesus taught.

Pharaoh's magicians, defeated at the third plague, say 'This is the finger of God.' Jesus uses the same expression to interpret His exorcisms, and so Luke invites readers to hear in the mute man's release an echo of the Exodus: God is again breaking the power of a tyrant to free His people.

The parallel to verse 20 reads 'Spirit of God' where Luke has 'finger of God.' Together they teach that the kingdom has come through the same divine power that is both the creator's hand and the Spirit, and they invite us to see Luke's wording as a deliberate Exodus allusion.

The prophet asks whether plunder can be taken from a mighty man, and God answers that He will retrieve the captives of the tyrant. The strong man parable in verses 21 and 22 gives the answer from the other side: yes, when someone stronger comes. Jesus is the one in whom that promise is kept.

The Ninevites believed God and put on sackcloth from the greatest to the least. Jesus uses this response of a pagan city against the people who hear a greater preacher and do not repent. The comparison condemns resistance by pointing at those who ought to have known less and responded more.

Zechariah, the priest's son, is stoned in the courtyard of the LORD's house after warning the people, and he cries that the LORD will see and avenge. This is the last murder of the Hebrew Bible's order, which makes verse 51's 'from Abel to Zechariah' a statement about the whole Scripture.

Anyone who touches a grave is unclean for seven days. Jesus' picture of leaders as 'unmarked graves' that people walk over without noticing turns their ritual care upside down: the very people who guard purity are spreading uncleanness.

The LORD tells Samuel that He does not see as man sees, for man sees the outward appearance but the LORD sees the heart. The same principle sits behind Jesus' diagnosis of the clean cup and the full inside, and shows that the Pharisees' fault was a very old one.

Jesus says His mother and brothers are those who hear the word of God and carry it out. In 11:27 and 28 He gives the same answer to the woman who blesses His mother. The two sayings together make hearing and obeying the word, rather than family ties or admiration, the mark of blessedness.

study.oneStory:
The chapter picks up a theme that began in the garden. Humanity was made to walk with God as children with a Father, and sin broke that relationship, so that people hid, covered themselves and doubted His goodness, Genesis 3:8-10. The Lord's Prayer is the way back: a short prayer that restores the confidence of a child. When Jesus tells His followers to say 'Father,' He is undoing the retreat from Genesis 3, and when He promises the Holy Spirit to those who ask, He is giving back what was lost, the presence of God with His people.

The chapter also tells the story of two kingdoms. From Genesis 3:15 Scripture has spoken of a war between the woman's seed and the serpent, and the Exodus showed that the finger of God can overturn a tyrant. In Luke 11 that war is visible in a mute man freed, and in a house taken from the strong man. The stronger one has come, and the remaining question is which side each hearer will take. The warning against the swept and empty house shows that the war is also internal, and that cleansing without filling is not salvation. Ezekiel 36:26-27 promised a new heart and the Spirit within, and the Father's gift of the Spirit in verse 13 is how that promise reaches the people who ask.

The chapter's judgment also belongs to the whole story. The blood of Abel cried out from the ground in Genesis 4:10, and the account of Zechariah in Chronicles closes the long record of the Hebrew Bible's martyrs. When Jesus says the account will be charged to 'this generation,' He is describing a reckoning that reaches its highest point in the cross, where the rejection of prophets culminates in the rejection of the Son. Yet the cross is also where the strong man is finally bound. The story ends in Revelation 22:3-4, where nothing accursed remains and God's servants see His face, and where the prayer that begins 'Your kingdom come' is finally answered.

sermon.title: “Lord, Teach Us to Pray”
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Luke, this message opens Luke 11 and the disciple's request, unfolding the privilege of addressing the sovereign and holy God as Father and the pattern Jesus gives for prayer. A faithful, expository handling of this movement's opening scene.

quiz.q: How did Jesus teach His disciples to begin their prayer?

options.text: By addressing God intimately as Father and asking that His name be hallowed and His kingdom come.
options.note: Luke 11:2 opens with Father, hallowed be Your name, Your kingdom come.

options.text: By first confessing a long list of their sins in detail.
options.note: Forgiveness is asked in the prayer, but Jesus begins with the Father and His name and kingdom, not with a catalog of sins.

options.text: By reciting the words with no thought, as a formula.
options.note: The prayer is a pattern to shape real trust, not a formula to repeat thoughtlessly.

options.text: By reminding God of their good works to earn a hearing.
options.note: Prayer here is the confident asking of children, not a bargain based on merit.

quiz.q: What is the best gift the Father gives to those who ask, according to Luke 11:13?

options.text: The Holy Spirit.
options.note: Luke uniquely names the Holy Spirit as the gift the Father gives to those who ask.

options.text: Good gifts of every kind for His children.
options.note: True that He gives good gifts, but Luke specifically climaxes with the Holy Spirit as the supreme gift.

options.text: Whatever we ask, exactly as we ask it.
options.note: The Father gives what is good, not a snake for a fish; the promise is qualified by His wisdom.

options.text: Freedom from ever needing to ask again.
options.note: Jesus urges continual asking, seeking, and knocking, not a one-time request.

quiz.q: What did Jesus say His casting out of demons proved?

options.text: That by the finger of God the kingdom of God had come upon them.
options.note: Luke 11:20 links His exorcisms to the arrival of God's kingdom.

options.text: That He was stronger than Satan and could plunder his house.
options.note: True from the strong man saying, but the stated conclusion is that the kingdom of God has come.

options.text: That signs from heaven were unnecessary for faith.
options.note: He does refuse to perform signs on demand, but the point of the exorcisms is the kingdom's arrival.

options.text: That He worked by the power of Beelzebul.
options.note: This is the slander Jesus refutes, not what His works proved.

quiz.q: What was wrong with the Pharisees in Jesus' woes?

options.text: They cleaned the outside while inside they were full of greed, neglecting justice and the love of God.
options.note: Luke 11:39-42 exposes clean outsides and unclean, unloving hearts.

options.text: They were too careful about tithing small herbs.
options.note: Jesus says they should have tithed without neglecting justice; the deeper fault was the neglected heart, not the tithing itself.

options.text: They refused to wash their hands before meals.
options.note: It was Jesus who skipped the washing; their fault was inner uncleanness, not a lapsed ritual.

options.text: They cared too much about justice and the love of God.
options.note: The opposite: they disregarded justice and the love of God.

quiz.q: What is the sign of Jonah that Jesus offers this generation?

options.text: The Son of Man's call to repentance, pointing to His death and resurrection, as Jonah was a sign to Nineveh.
options.note: Luke 11:29-32 makes Jonah a sign of repentance fulfilled in the Son of Man.

options.text: Jonah's preaching that led Nineveh to repent.
options.note: True to Luke's emphasis, but the sign points beyond Jonah to the Son of Man Himself, greater than Jonah.

options.text: A spectacular wonder from the sky on demand.
options.note: Jesus refuses exactly this; the only sign given is Jonah, not a sign from heaven.

options.text: Proof that this generation had nothing to answer for.
options.note: The sign leaves them without excuse, since One greater than Jonah is here.

questions: Jesus teaches us to pray simply, Father. How would your prayers change if you truly believed you were speaking to a good Father rather than a reluctant judge?
The friend at midnight kept knocking. Where have you stopped asking God for something because the door has stayed shut so far?
The Father delights to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. When did you last ask God not merely for things but for more of His own presence and power?
Jesus warns against a life swept clean but left empty. Is there a sin you have merely tidied away rather than replaced with Christ Himself?
The Pharisees kept the outside of the cup shining while the inside was full of greed. Where might your public appearance be outrunning the state of your heart?

translationNotes.note: Luke preserves a shorter form of the Lord's Prayer. Many later manuscripts expand it toward Matthew's fuller version, adding Our Father in heaven, Your will be done on earth as in heaven, and deliver us from the evil one; the BSB places these in footnotes as absent from the earliest witnesses.

The finger of God deliberately echoes Exodus 8:19, where the magicians recognize God's power in the plagues. Jesus casts His exorcisms as a new act of divine deliverance and the inbreaking of the kingdom.

From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah spans, in the Hebrew ordering of the Old Testament, its first and last martyrs, that is, the whole record of the prophets' blood, charged against a generation that rejects its Messiah.
